content:
You are about to sign a construction contract, and once your signature is on it, your leverage changes completely. Before that moment, ask questions. After it, you live with the answers.

We have reviewed enough contracts with homeowners to know exactly where the gaps hide. Here is what to check before you sign anything.

Confirm the License and Insurance First

This is the single most important check, and it takes only a few minutes. Ask for the contractor's license number and verify it directly with your state licensing board, not just by taking their word for it.

Insurance matters just as much. A contractor without active liability insurance leaves you exposed if something goes wrong on your property during construction, including injury to a worker on site.

Read the Scope of Work Carefully

A vague scope of work is where budget disputes are born. The contract should describe exactly what is included, down to specific materials, finishes, and fixtures, not general language like standard finishes throughout.

What a Clear Scope Includes

  • Specific materials and brands, not vague placeholder terms
  • Exact square footage or room dimensions being worked on
  • A list of what is explicitly excluded from the project
  • Who is responsible for permits and inspection scheduling
  • A defined process for handling change orders mid project

If any of these are missing, ask for them in writing before signing. Verbal promises do not hold up when a dispute happens later.

Check the Payment Schedule Structure

How you pay matters as much as how much you pay. A payment schedule tied to project milestones protects you far more than one that front loads payment before work begins.

I always advise clients to be cautious of any contract asking for more than a small deposit upfront. Reasonable payment schedules release funds as specific stages complete: after permits are approved, after framing, after rough electrical and plumbing, and a final payment only once the punch list is fully resolved.

Understand the Timeline and Delay Clauses

Every contract should include a realistic project timeline with a start date and estimated completion date. More importantly, it should explain what happens if the timeline slips.

Look for language addressing delays caused by weather, material shortages, or permit approval times, since these are common in construction. What matters is who is accountable if delays happen without a valid reason, and whether the contract includes any protection for you as the homeowner in that scenario.

Warranty Terms Deserve Real Attention

A written warranty is one of the clearest signs a contractor stands behind their work. Vague language like industry standard warranty applies means very little if a problem shows up after the project ends.

Ask exactly what the warranty covers, how long it lasts, and what the process looks like if something needs to be fixed. A specific, written warranty with a clear timeframe protects you far better than a verbal assurance made during the sales conversation.

A Real Contract Dispute, Start to Finish

A homeowner in Tampa signed a contract with vague scope language describing kitchen finishes as standard grade materials. Once construction began, the contractor installed the lowest cost cabinetry available, technically fulfilling the contract while completely missing what the homeowner expected.

The dispute took weeks to resolve and required a change order with additional cost to upgrade to the materials the homeowner had originally pictured. A specific, written scope of work at signing would have prevented the entire disagreement.

The Simplest Way to Protect Yourself

I prioritize a strategy where every contract we write includes a detailed scope, a milestone based payment schedule, a realistic timeline, and clear warranty terms before a homeowner ever signs. Our build services team walks through every line of the contract during the initial consultation, so there are no surprises hidden in vague language.

If your project also involves design work, our earlier guide on permit ready drawings explains why approved plans should exist before a contract is finalized, not after construction begins.

Final Thoughts

A construction contract protects whoever wrote it more carefully. Confirm the license and insurance, demand a specific scope of work, check the payment schedule, understand the timeline terms, and get the warranty in writing. These five checks take an afternoon and can save you months of frustration later.

faqs.q: What should I check first before signing a construction contract?
faqs.a: Verify the contractor's license and insurance directly with your state licensing board before reviewing any other part of the contract.

faqs.q: How much deposit is reasonable for a construction project?
faqs.a: A reasonable deposit is typically a small percentage of the total project cost, with the remaining balance tied to completed milestones.

faqs.q: What should a scope of work include?
faqs.a: It should list specific materials, dimensions, exclusions, and responsibilities for permits, not general or vague descriptions of the work.

faqs.q: What happens if my contractor misses the project timeline?
faqs.a: A well written contract addresses accountability for delays not caused by weather or permitting, protecting you from open ended timelines.

faqs.q: Is a verbal warranty enough protection?
faqs.a: No. A warranty should be written into the contract with a specific duration and clear terms for what is covered.
